title: Change money there and back
hook: You swap dollars to euros and straight back. Does the same amount come home?

doesNotKnow: that buying and selling rates differ
that a round trip loses money even if the market does not move

misconception: Exchange the money there and back and I end with the same.
objective: The learner can explain that the gap between a booth's buy and sell rates is a cost paid on a round trip: $1,000 at 0.90 euro per dollar and $1.05 per euro returns $945.

claims.text: At 0.90 euro per dollar, $1,000 becomes 900 euros.
Selling those 900 euros back at $1.05 per euro returns $945, a loss of $55 with no market move.
Getting the full $1,000 back would take 1 / 0.90 = 1.1111 dollars per euro on the way back, which means no gap between the two rates.
claims.source: 1,000 = 900 x p gives p = 1.1111. Demo.tsx BREAK_EVEN.

claims.text: The gap between a booth's buy and sell rates is a cost paid whenever you cross.
claims.source: Standard definition of a bid-ask spread in currency exchange; the loss on the stage is the arithmetic of the two invented rates.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: one booth, two invented rates, no fees, no market movement, and no advice on where to change money.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: one booth, invented rates, no fees'.

recall.question: A booth gives 0.80 euro per dollar and sells dollars at $1.20 per euro. You change $500 to euros and straight back. What do you hold?
recall.why: 500 x 0.80 = 400 euros; 400 x 1.20 = $480. The gap between the two rates is lost on the round trip.
